RV & van life · US 120 V

Best power station for an RV air conditioner

Every machine below is ranked by a calculation, not by an opinion: whether it can even absorb this rooftop unit’s start-up current — the single largest instantaneous demand this library has measured, soft-start accessories aside — whether its brand publishes enough to prove how long it lasts, whether it can be bought today, and then price.

Nothing in this region’s library runs this set, so there is no recommendation to make. The rows below show what each machine ran out of.

What would change this

What changes this answer is not a bigger battery. Every refusal on this page is at the same instant — the compressor’s start — and that instant is a property of the air conditioner, not of the machine feeding it. A soft starter is fitted to the rooftop unit and moves that one number; because our verdict is a calculation rather than a lookup, moving it flips the result. The article below runs the same engine over the same records twice, once with a soft starter declared as fitted and once without, and states plainly what is modelled rather than measured. See what a soft starter changes

The rule is written out under the pick, the load is itemised with its figure’s source, and every row links to the calculator with that machine and this air conditioner already filled in — so you can re-run any number on this page yourself.

How this list is ordered

Four gates, applied in this order to every published US record. There is no score and no weighting — each gate either separates two machines or hands them to the next one.

  1. 1 Does it run the set?

    Every record is put through the compatibility engine against all of the loads at once — running watts against continuous output, the worst start-up instant against the surge ceiling, waveform where a load demands one. Green first, then the tight fits, then anything the engine could not read, then the machines that cannot do it. A machine that cannot start the load in front of it is not a cheaper option.

  2. 2 Can we prove how long?

    A runtime is only printed where the brand publishes what it takes to compute one — a usable-capacity coefficient, whether stated as depth of discharge and inverter efficiency or as one combined figure — and never from the number on the box. Records that reach the target sort first, records with a proven but shorter figure next (longest first: inside that band none of them does the job, so the one that gets closest wins), and records whose duration cannot be proven at all sort last inside their verdict band. That is a statement about published data, not about the hardware, and each of those rows says so.

  3. 3 Can it be bought today?

    A record under a verified out-of-stock policy, or one we may not sell into your state, sorts behind an equivalent one that can be bought. It stays on the list with the reason attached rather than disappearing. Whether WattPair happens to hold a purchase link for a record is not part of this gate and never moves it: a machine we cannot link to is ranked exactly as if we could, and simply carries no buy button.

  4. 4 Then price.

    Cheapest first, inside everything above. One mains standard and one currency per page, so every comparison is like for like. A record with no verified price sorts to the back of its own band — the absence of a price is not a low price.

The loads this ranks against

A single RV rooftop air conditioner, on its own — the load with the best-documented electrical data in this whole library (its manufacturer publishes the compressor’s locked-rotor current directly, not a derived estimate) and, on that same data, the hardest one for a portable power station to start. Mixing in the rest of a rig would only obscure which single number is deciding every row on this page.

The load that changes the answer

Add a 12V portable fridge/freezer to the same set and the first gate, which was already refusing every record here, goes on refusing them: not one of the 12 clears it outright — none is a tight fit and 12 cannot do it at all. The reason is one instant: a 12V portable fridge/freezer asks for 180 W at start-up on its own, against 8,619 W for everything on the list above put together. There is no locked-rotor rating behind that figure to quote: the compressor runs at variable speed, its own inverter board ramps it up rather than throwing it across the line, and its data sheet carries no locked-rotor column at all. There is no “before” to contrast against here — every record already fails on the air conditioner alone, by a wide margin. What would actually move this list is not another appliance; it is a soft starter, which the unit’s own installer documentation credits with cutting this exact current by up to three-quarters. The quiz carries this set as a preset.

Questions people ask about this list

Does anything here run it at all?
No — not one of the 12, and that is the finding on this page rather than a caveat to it. 1,690 W of running draw and 8,619 W at the worst start-up instant is what every published US record is measured against, and none of them holds it — the binding checks are continuous output and surge ceiling. Which means the buying question on this page is not “how long” but “what would have to change”, and the ranked list above says what each machine ran out of.
Why is the biggest machine not first?
It never gets there: nothing in this region’s library starts this load at all, so no machine — biggest or otherwise — reaches the point in the ranking where capacity would decide the order. The verdict column above states what each one ran out of.
How far short is it — is anything close?
Not close, and the shortfall is at one instant rather than across the run. These units publish a compressor locked-rotor current model by model in the installer’s own unit-data table: 52.0 to 68.0 A on the 13,500 Btu/h class and 60.0 to 70.0 A on the 15,000, which at 120 V is 6,240 to 8,400 VA. That is the hardest surge data in this library — a manufacturer measurement rather than a category estimate — and it is what every refusal above is measured against. Two further figures make the picture worse rather than better: the fan motor carries its own locked-rotor rating of 5.6 to 10.0 A that is not in that total, and the running draw is a weather figure, 1,690 W at the 95 °F rating condition and 2,050 W at 120 °F outdoors.
